articles.title: Cheltenham theatre centre 'vitally important', says Josh O'Connor
articles.summary: Actor Josh O'Connor says his new hometown theatre education centre is "incredibly important".
articles.body:
BAFTA-nominated actor Josh O'Connor says a new theatre education centre in his hometown is "vitally important" for young, aspiring actors.

O'Connor, who is reported to be in the running to be the next James Bond , officially opened the new £1m Everyman Theatre education centre in Cheltenham, where he grew up, earlier.

The centre sits in a former community venue and will be used to help give everyone access to the performing arts.

O'Connor, who attended Everyman's youth theatre, said: "It's an incredible gift to be able to learn to do drama."

The Crown star Josh O'Connor reacts to Bond rumours

Home births to resume as maternity unit to reopen

Firework displays cancelled over concerns for animals

He said the space was a "great opportunity for young people and old people and everyone in between".

The 36-year-old actor, who played Prince Charles in Netflix's The Crown, spent a lot of time growing up at the former Axiom arts centre in the town, describing it as "an amazing space for learning the arts and crafts".

A number of attempts were made to revive it before the borough council sold it in 2005.

O'Connor, a former Bristol Old Vic Theatre School student, said the Axiom "left a big hole in the community".

"I think there's a shortage of community spaces," added O'Connor, who worked at a local Waitrose before starring alongside Daniel Craig in the film Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery.

Charis, 17, from Cheltenham, started at Everyman's youth theatre aged seven and is hoping to study musical theatre at university.

She said the theatre had "changed my life around for the better".

She was diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis, a disorder that damages your lungs, digestive tract and other organs, at nine years old.

Charis said the diagnosis "really flipped my life upside down" but the youth theatre was "a big escape".

Charis came to the new centre for classes over the summer and said it was a place where she could feel herself because she was "surrounded by people that I've got to know and doing the thing I love with".

It cost £1m to buy and refurbish the building in Grove Street and make it a permanent base for the theatre's Education and Community Department.

But the theatre needs to raise a further £170,000 per year to keep it open.

Chief executive Mark Goucher said: "Our job is now to keep it running and keep it open... so that we can carry on delivering great work down here."

Free and heavily subsidised arts and culture projects such as youth choirs and family clubs will be offered at the venue.

Goucher said the project was about "giving opportunities to children who may not necessarily have had those opportunities".

They have plans to add more choirs, as well as dance classes for older people and sessions for people with dementia.

"We're doing the right thing and the theatre changes people's lives, and that's what I think Grove Street will do as well," added Goucher.

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial next month
articles.summary: Mountbatten-Windsor has been summonsed to give evidence in a businessman's High Court fraud trial.
articles.body:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December, the BBC understands

The witness summons will see him giving evidence and taking questions, in a case in which a wealthy woman alleges she was cheated by her former financial adviser.

Mountbatten-Windsor is not accused of wrongdoing, but he could face difficult questions about his financial arrangements as it is said that he was in receipt of some of the disputed payments, including a transfer to him of £750,000.

His court appearance will be the first public questioning Mountbatten-Windsor has faced since his BBC Newsnight interview in 2019.

It is also believed that Mountbatten-Windsor is the first royal since the 19th Century to be sent such a witness summons.

Such an unusual royal moment is likely to receive widespread media coverage - not least for the opportunity to hear the former Duke of York's first public comments since being stripped of his titles.

The summons was issued this week, with the case set to begin from mid-November and with Mountbatten-Windsor to appear as a witness around the 15 December, which is usually in person, but could be on video.

There have been many questions in recent years about Mountbatten-Windsor's personal finances - and challenges about a lack of transparency - and this case promises to give a rare opportunity to hear his own explanations about his financial dealings.

The case will hear allegations made by Nebahat Isbilen, an elderly Turkish woman, who says her former adviser Selman Turk misled her and used her wealth to his own advantage.

Mountbatten-Windsor will be asked to give evidence related to disputed questions about the handling of Isbilen's money.

According to court documents, Isbilen claimed she was misled by Turk into paying £750,000 to Mountbatten-Windsor, believing it was for help with a passport.

Turk has denied the allegation and says this payment was a gift made on Isbilen's own initiative to create goodwill with the then duke and had nothing to do with a passport.

The case covers payments made at the very end of his time as a working royal.

The transfer of money came the day after Mountbatten-Windsor recorded his BBC Newsnight interview, which was then broadcast the following night, and was soon followed by the then Duke of York stepping down from royal duties.

In 2021, Isbilen's lawyers contacted the then Prince Andrew and the money had been paid back, but the forthcoming court case will consider claims about Turk's behaviour, with Mountbatten-Windsor set to be a significant witness.

Court documents show there will be questions about another significant sum of money paid from Isbilen's account - around £768,000 in January 2020.

Turk has claimed it was a loan to Mountbatten-Windsor for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland - a suggestion which is contested by Isbilen and had been challenged in previous court hearings.

Turk had met Mountbatten-Windsor in autumn 2019 through the Pitch@Palace project, a Dragon's Den-style pitching event run by the former duke.

That had led to social gatherings, bringing together Turk and his family, Isbilen and the then Duke and Duchess of York.

Justice Adam Johnson has said that, given the seriousness of the allegations, Turk should have access to "the evidence he considers relevant and material".

That meant that Turk wanted to use Mountbatten-Windsor's evidence and has been successful in summonsing him for that purpose.

Turk's representatives, Janes Solicitors, said he denies the claims of dishonesty and looks forward to being vindicated in court.

Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for a response.

The trial at the High Court is expected to begin later this month.

articles.title: A father left 4.75 acres of mostly swampy land to his 12 children in 1995; one daughter said he had promised her the hill section, and the Privy Council set aside an order to demolish her nearly completed house
articles.summary: In December 1995, a father in Trinidad made a will leaving 4.75 acres of mainly swampy, undeveloped land to his twelve children in equal shares.
articles.body: In December 1995, a father in Trinidad made a will leaving 4.75 acres of mainly swampy, undeveloped land to his twelve children in equal shares. His daughter, Vashti Ramlal, said he had promised her the section known as the Land on the Hill. On 23 February 2026, the Privy Council, in a judgment by Lord Briggs, upheld the trial judge's finding that the promise was made, but held that no case of proprietary estoppel was open to her. The Board also set aside the Court of Appeal's order to demolish a nearly completed house, describing the order as "completely unexplained".Privy Council reviews dispute over promised hill land and house demolitionLord Briggs states that the dispute became contentious because Vashti's siblings, other than Chandra, were concerned that Vashti's family was claiming more than her share. He records that nine of the children issued a claim in November 2016 against Vashti, Omar and their son Ravi, seeking damages for trespass, demolition of a new house, and removal of fencing and belongings from the Land on the Hill. The judgment says Ravi had demolished the Chattel House in February 2016 and begun building the New House on the same spot. The defendants counterclaimed for a declaration that Vashti owned the Land on the Hill.The trial judge, Margaret Mohammed J, dismissed the trespass claim and declared Vashti the owner of the Land on the Hill. According to the Privy Council, she accepted evidence from Vashti, and from Chandra, that the Deceased had told Chandra when making the will to ensure Vashti received that land as her share. The Court of Appeal, by a majority of Bereaux and Wilson JJA, held that this finding could not stand, mainly because in their view the will was inconsistent with it. Lord Briggs notes that the majority nevertheless dismissed both the claim and the counterclaim, and ordered that the New House, by then nearly completed, be demolished. Rajkumar JA dissented on the question of the promise.Court upholds daughter's claim to father's promise over inherited landThe Board concluded that the Court of Appeal should not have overturned the trial judge's finding of fact that the Deceased promised Vashti the Land on the Hill as her share upon her parents' death. Lord Briggs explains that there was an inconsistency in legal effect between the will and such a promise, because a devise to several people in equal shares gives each an undivided share in the whole. But he states that there was not such an inconsistency in fact as to require the judge to reject the evidence of Vashti and Chandra. The judgment says the Deceased appears to have assumed that the will and his instruction to Chandra would fulfil the earlier promise, and that the fact the assumption was wrong does not mean he did not make it. A survey provided after the Court of Appeal's judgment showed the Land on the Hill to be a little less than 1/12 of the whole in area.On proprietary estoppel, Lord Briggs agrees with the Court of Appeal that the promise, the instruction to Chandra and the will did not make an effective gift, describing it as an imperfect gift that equity does not perfect without more. He records that no case of proprietary estoppel was pleaded or pursued at trial and that it was advanced for the first time on appeal. The judgment also states that reliance is an essential element and that it was not pleaded, found or proved that Vashti and Omar acted as they did because of the promise. The Board found it unfair for the claim to be raised for the first time on appeal, since the respondents had no opportunity to raise their own points. It therefore agreed that the defendants had not established a case for equitable relief. The Board also declined to grant a declaration of the Deceased's promise, saying that the Board had already made clear that the judge's finding was upheld.Board urges mediation after overturning house demolition orderLord Briggs records that in written submissions to the Court of Appeal on 28 September 2023 the claimants stated that, in the spirit of compromise, none of them wished the house to be pulled down. The judgment says a survey by L&S Surveying Services Ltd then reported that the area occupied by Vashti's family, including the whole footprint of the New House, was less than 1/12 of the land in area. The Court of Appeal's order of 8 December 2023 nonetheless required the structure to be pulled down, without reasons and without reference to those submissions or the survey. Before the Board, the judgment notes, the claimants' counsel said his instructions were that they did want the house pulled down, and the Board was told that the house had cost in excess of T&T$400,000 to build.The Board described the order as "completely unexplained" and set it aside. Lord Briggs states that the land will sooner or later have to be partitioned or sold, that any partition would only be fair if regard were had to shares of equal value rather than equal area, and that the house had been built with the consent of Chandra as legal owner. The appeal was allowed only to the limited extent of removing the Court of Appeal's declaration that the house was illegally constructed and its demolition injunction. The injunction prohibiting further construction continues until further order, and other matters concerning the parties' interests were remitted to a High Court judge in Trinidad and Tobago. The judgment records that the hearing took place on 9 December 2025 before Lord Reed, Lord Briggs, Lord Hamblen, Lord Leggatt and Lady Rose, and that the Board endorsed Rajkumar JA's advice that the dispute "cries out for mediation".You use AI every day. articles.title: Taoiseach pushes 'initiative' on the constitutional future of the island
articles.summary: The Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin is to set up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland.
articles.body:
The Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin is to set up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland.

It comes as the party's coalition partner, Fine Gael, is to unveil its plans for a "blueprint" on Irish unity at its ard fheis (annual party conference) this weekend in Cork.

He outlined his plans in a private meeting with his parliamentary party, Fianna Fáil, in Dublin on Tuesday.

The Taoiseach's Futures Study Initiative will "seek to provide an objective, independent knowledge base which can be used to inform specific proposals", according to a policy document produced by Martin in the meeting.

Each political party and activist group will be invited to make submissions.

The initiative will also give unionists and loyalists, as well as nationalists, an opportunity to have their say.

"In this it would provide a good faith opportunity for those outside the nationalist tradition to participate.

"Critically, it would challenge all traditions to move from making general assertions about the future to engaging with hard evidence," the policy paper, seen by BBC News NI, says.

A single "unitary republic" which will be governed by institutions primarily based in Dublin which would be fully in place within five years of a referendum on a United Ireland, without a devolved government in Northern Ireland

A United Ireland, or an "all-island state", with a devolved government in Northern Ireland similar to the one in place now

A continuation of the current arrangements in the Good Friday Agreement without constitutional change

The initiative will not recommend a single proposal but instead explore the specific impacts and requirements of three core scenarios for the constitutional future of the island.

It will then produce a report to the Irish government which will be published.

The group will explore six main areas which are "critical" to the future of the island: constitutional and legal change, economy, health, education, security, symbols and culture.

The initiative will be led by a chairperson and at least five people, with their work overseen by experts in the fields in which they explore.

A "dedicated secretariat" should be established in the Department of the Taoiseach for the process, according to the policy paper, which should include a mix of public service expertise and outside specialists.

The policy paper adds that "nothing" in the initiative "interferes with or seeks to replace current commitments which we have towards active cooperation North/South and Ireland/UK under the Good Friday Agreement."

The Fianna Fáil parliamentary party is to hold a dedicated meeting on the issue in the coming weeks.

articles.title: 50 years after Harpeth River Jane Doe was found dead, investigators still hope to identify her
articles.summary: On March 24, 1976, the body of a teenage girl was found in the Harpeth River in Nashville, Tennessee. The Metropolitan Nashville Police Department is still trying to identify her.
articles.body: March 24, 1976. A fisherman found a body in the Harpeth River near the McCrory Lane Bridge in Nashville, Tennessee. The victim was a teenage girl. According to the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department (MNPD), investigators determined that the girl had drowned within hours of her body being discovered. Her manner of death was undetermined. In the back pocket of her blue jeans was a photo of a young boy. On the back of the photo was the name “Little Charley” and a phone number. Investigators called the number. A man named Charles Moore answered the phone. And so began a decades-long investigation to give Harpeth River Jane Doe her name back. Who was Harpeth River Jane Doe? Dateline spoke with Investigator Matthew Filter of the MNPD’s Cold Case Unit. “I’ve been aware of this case for a long time,” he said. Filter worked the Harpeth River Jane Doe case as a detective before retiring from the MNPD in December 2025. In August 2026, he returned as a part-time investigator and technical specialist. Harpeth River Jane Doe was estimated to be between 14 and 17 years old. Her blood alcohol content was 0.28% at the time of her death. “She was extremely intoxicated,” Filter said. According to Filter, there were indications of sexual activity, but no signs of sexual assault. Because the manner of death was undetermined, the teen’s case is being investigated as a homicide. “And there’s some suspicious circumstances,” Filter said. The location of the body was extremely remote. “It’s kinda hard for me to believe that she was out there all by herself.” To try to figure out how Harpeth River Jane Doe ended up alone in a remote part of Nashville, Filter has gone back to the beginning to review the 50-year-old case file. The Initial Investigation In March 1976, MNPD investigators contacted the man whose phone number was on the back of the photo found in the teen’s pocket, Nashville resident Charles Moore. They asked him what he knew about the Harpeth River Jane Doe. According to Filter, he said he recognized her. According to MNPD, Moore told investigators that he and his brother-in-law picked up two girls hitchhiking along I-24 on the south side of Nashville on March 15, 1976. One of them was Harpeth River Jane Doe. The two men drove the girls south to the Winchester exit, “roughly about a 45-minute to an hour drive, depending on how fast they were going,” Filter said. Moore told investigators that the girls said they were traveling from up north. “They said they were coming from somewhere up north of Minnesota,” Filter said. “That’s where they were living, and they were just going down to Florida.” Moore told investigators that Harpeth River Jane Doe told him her name was Sherry, and that she and her friend had been institutionalized up north. “The Harpeth Doe told them that she was in a facility for alcoholism, and the other girl claimed that she was institutionalized because she had apparently tried to commit suicide,” Filter said. It was a lead, but according to Filter, investigators came up empty after sending teletypes seeking information about runaways or missing persons in Minnesota. “They pretty much exhausted everything that they were able to,” Filter said. Investigators have also been unable to identify the girl who was traveling with Harpeth River Jane Doe. According to Filter, Moore told investigators that the photograph they found in Harpeth River Jane Doe’s pocket was of her companion’s child. The young boy in the photograph has never been identified. Moore told investigators that he had given the girls his phone number in case they needed another ride. It was the same number found on the back of the little boy’s photograph. “I think they kind of alluded that they may be coming back up this way,” Filter said. Throughout the investigation, Moore was treated as a cooperating witness by investigators. “I did not get the impression that he really had anything to do with her death,” Filter said. Investigators don’t know what happened to the two girls after Moore and his brother-in-law dropped them off. According to Filter, Moore said he never heard from them again. Supposedly, they “started hitchhiking right there on the exit and got picked up a short time later by another truck and continued going south,” Filter said. Nine days later, Harpeth River Jane Doe’s body was found back in Nashville. “We really don’t have any idea what -- what transpired between the time they dropped her off at the Winchester exit and her body was found,” Filter said. The Cemetery More than 50 years have passed. Advances in DNA technology have made genetic genealogy a promising option for identifying Harpeth River Jane Doe. There’s only one problem. “We’re not really sure where the body is buried,” Filter told Dateline. Records show that Jane Doe was buried in Davidson County Cemetery in North Nashville. The cemetery served indigent residents until the early 1980s and is still maintained by the Metro Park Service. According to Filter, at some point the grave markers were disturbed. “They had just gotten knocked around, and nobody really knew if the markers were in the right place,” Filter said. “So now you just got this field, and you don’t know where anybody is.” Filter says he’s conducted research into the indigent burial program. Although records show when Jane Doe was buried and who buried her, the location of her burial plot can’t be identified without the grave markers. And without a certain location, exhumation isn’t possible. “To get that exhumation order signed by a judge, we have to be able to say with 100% certainty that this is exactly where she’s buried,” he said. “That’s where we’re running into a lot of problems.” Enter River Robbins In 2020, during the COVID lockdown, Nashville resident River Robbins started looking into local cold cases. The Harpeth River Jane Doe case was already on Robbins’s radar when he saw it on the Nashville cold case website and decided to do a deep dive. “Just tried to gather as much information as I could on what was publicly available at the time,” Robbins told Dateline. Robbins’s research has primarily focused on locating Harpeth River Jane Doe’s burial site in Davidson County Cemetery. He told Dateline he found a photograph taken during her burial published in the Nashville Banner. By comparing it to aerial images of the cemetery taken over the years, Robbins says he has been able to narrow down where she might be buried using the surrounding tree lines and landscape. Robbins says he has confirmed the identities of 2,574 people buried in Davidson County Cemetery after combing through death certificates and available cemetery records. He still has 26 years of death certificates to go through. “I have forecasted I will end up with roughly 3,600-4,000 confirmed burials by the time my research is complete,” he said. An essential part of Robbins’s research involves locating the cemetery’s original grave markers. In October 2026, Robbins conducted a search in the cemetery for remaining markers. He was joined by forensic anthropologist Dr. Tiffany Fracchia, an associate professor of anthropology at Vanderbilt University, archaeologist Dr. Adam Fracchia, Investigator Filter and Detective Andrew Davis of the MNPD’s Cold Case Unit. Using a metal detector in the area they believe Harpeth River Jane Doe is buried, the group found a row of grave markers approximately six inches underground. According to Robbins, they also discovered other markers that appeared to have been scattered. “The next step is to scientifically map this,” Fracchia said. “We’re hoping that what we would be able to do is kind of count through, based on the records and the archives that Robbins has identified, and be able to count to the plot where we believe Harpeth River Jane Doe is buried.” Fracchia is working with professors in Vanderbilt’s geospatial department to secure grant funding for ground-penetrating radar and other imaging technology to map Davidson County Cemetery. “Our goal would be to get work immediately,” she said. “Harpeth River Jane Doe has been waiting a long time to be identified.” For Fracchia, the project is about more than identifying Harpeth River Jane Doe. It’s also about remembering the thousands of others buried in the cemetery. “There have been several people historically who have kind of taken up that mantle to try to make sure that these people are not forgotten,” she told Dateline. “And so I really think it’s our turn now.” Who was Harpeth River Jane Doe’s Friend? Another potential key to unlocking Harpeth River Jane Doe’s identity lies in identifying her travel companion. One clue Robbins was particularly interested in was the photo of the young boy found in Harpeth River Jane Doe’s pocket. Filter says the original photo was lost. Through newspaper archives, Robbins learned that in April 1976, an inmate in a Nashville jail claimed he had spoken to Harpeth River Jane Doe at a local bar. The inmate said she told him she was from Columbus, Georgia. “Nashville police actually sent a scan of the photo to a newspaper in Columbus,” he said. “The Ledger-Enquirer there ran a copy of it.” According to Robbins, the lead went cold, and investigators at the time told the press that they believed the lead to be false. Robbins obtained a copy of the photograph from the Ledger-Enquirer, which he describes as “a scan of a scan of a scan.” He hopes someone will recognize the photograph and help identify Harpeth River Jane Doe’s companion. “Maybe someone out there would recognize the photo,” he said. Investigators have explored the possibility that Harpeth River Jane Doe’s travel companion was also found dead. In April 1976, an unidentified girl’s body was found in Crittenden, Kentucky, about 250 miles from Nashville. “I think it was two or three weeks after the Harpeth River Doe was found,” Filter said. The girl became known as Grant County Jane Doe. According to Filter, the Kentucky medical examiner believed the girl had been dead for two to three weeks before she was found. “Which would have put her time -- her death date around the same time as Harpeth Doe’s,” he said. When Filter showed Charles Moore a forensic rendering of Grant County Jane Doe, Moore told him it resembled the girl who had been traveling with Harpeth River Jane Doe. Kentucky investigators have been unable to identify Grant County Jane Doe using DNA for the same reason as their Nashville counterparts. “They know what cemetery this girl is buried in, but they don’t know where in the cemetery because all the markers are gone,” Filter said. What’s Next… “If we’re able to get her identified, that’s gonna answer a whole lot of questions for us,” Filter said. “I always hold out hope that any of these cases can be solved.” In fact, this wouldn’t be the first Jane Doe cold case that Investigator Filter helped solve. Dateline interviewed him in 2025 when we covered the case of Vandy Jane Doe in our “Cold Case Spotlight” series. A year later, the MNPD announced that Vandy Jane Doe had been identified as 25-year-old Yadezia Jones of Nashville. They are now working to solve her case. The Harpeth River Jane Doe case has also inspired Robbins, a crime and fiction writer, to pursue a new career. “What’s crazy is this case actually, back in 2020, got me thinking about pursuing a degree in law enforcement or criminal justice,” he said. In May 2026, he graduated with a criminal justice degree. “My dream job is to be a cold case detective,” he said. Robbins continues to be a passionate advocate for Harpeth River Jane Doe. “Even though it’s been 50 years,” he said, “there’s a good chance that she still has siblings, potentially parents, some type of family member or friend that is still alive that might recognize her.” “If we can figure out who she is and give her family that closure and give her her name back, I think that is above all the most important thing,” he said. Filter also hopes to identify Harpeth River Jane Doe and provide answers to her family, whoever they may be. He hopes that identifying her will ultimately help investigators determine what happened to her. “I would want them to know that we’re still doing everything we can think of to try to locate her and get her identified and get her returned back to you,” he said. Harpeth River Jane Doe is believed to have been between 14 and 17 years old at the time of her death. Her ethnicity is listed by the MNPD as White/Caucasian/Latino/Native American. She was 5’2” and 120 lbs., with brown hair and brown eyes. She had a mole on her left temple, two surgical scars on her abdomen, and old scars, possibly from cigarette burns, on both arms. When her body was found, she was wearing blue jeans, a bra, a choker-type necklace with beads and a white dove, and a rawhide bracelet. Anyone with information about Harpeth River Jane Doe’s identity or case should contact the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department Cold Case Unit at 615-862-7329. articles.title: Seth Rogen and his wife founded an Alzheimer’s charity after her mother’s diagnosis; by 2025, its programmes had reached 4.4 million people and supported families with respite care
articles.summary: For Seth Rogen and his wife, Lauren Miller Rogen, Alzheimer’s disease became a personal concern long before it became the focus of their charitable work.
articles.body: For Seth Rogen and his wife, Lauren Miller Rogen, Alzheimer’s disease became a personal concern long before it became the focus of their charitable work. Lauren’s mother was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s, an experience that eventually led the couple to establish an organisation supporting families affected by the condition. Their charity, Hilarity for Charity (HFC), has since developed programmes covering caregiver assistance, brain health education and research into prevention. Its 2025 annual report records a year of expanded outreach, with 4.4 million people reached through its programmes, events and online community. The organisation also provided thousands of hours of relief for people caring for loved ones at home.How Lauren Miller Rogen’s family experience led to Hilarity for CharityThe story behind Hilarity for Charity began with Lauren Miller Rogen’s family. Her mother, Adele Miller, was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, bringing the effects of the condition into the couple’s personal lives. Rather than limiting their involvement to raising awareness, Seth and Lauren decided to build an organisation that could help people dealing with similar circumstances.They established Hilarity for Charity in 2012, using comedy and entertainment to bring attention to a disease that affects both patients and the people who care for them. Seth Rogen’s public profile helped attract audiences, while Lauren became closely involved in developing the organisation’s work. Its activities gradually expanded beyond fundraising events to include practical assistance for caregivers, educational initiatives and support for brain health research.The organisation's approach recognises that Alzheimer’s affects entire families. Relatives often take on substantial responsibilities as a person's memory and ability to manage everyday activities decline. Finding time for work, household responsibilities and personal needs can become difficult for those providing care.Respite grants and emergency aid form a key part of HFC’s workOne of HFC’s main areas of work is helping family caregivers obtain temporary breaks from their responsibilities. Its Caregiver Respite Grant Programme provides financial assistance that can be used to arrange care for a loved one, allowing relatives to step away for a period without leaving the person unsupported.According to its 2025 annual report, the organisation awarded 200 respite care grants, representing 26,000 hours of care. Its headline figures also record more than 550,000 hours of in-home care relief awarded through the programme. These figures appear as separate measures in the report, with the 26,000 hours referring to grants awarded during the year.HFC also provided emergency assistance to families facing sudden financial difficulties. In 2025, it distributed 18 emergency grants worth more than $43,000 in direct support. The assistance followed events including the Los Angeles wildfires and flooding in North Carolina, when some caregivers and families affected by dementia faced additional disruption.The organisation said its response developed into a wider commitment to helping families manage unexpected circumstances. Its partnership with the Judy Jane Foundation helped support this work.Support groups give caregivers a place to share their experiencesFinancial assistance is only one part of the support HFC offers. The organisation also runs weekly groups where caregivers can discuss the demands of looking after someone with Alzheimer’s or another form of dementia.In 2025, approximately 500 caregivers took part in 37 weekly support groups. The sessions included dedicated spaces for different communities and circumstances, including Black, Indigenous and people of colour (BIPOC) caregivers, bereaved caregivers, LGBTQIA+ families and Spanish-speaking participants. There were also groups for people caring for someone with frontotemporal dementia (FTD).HFC reported that around 300 caregivers also participated in more than 70 Caregiver Community Lounges. These gatherings covered different aspects of caregiving and offered opportunities for people to exchange information and discuss challenges with others in similar situations.The organisation has also begun extending its respite care work into adult day services and support for professional caregivers. This reflects an effort to reach beyond relatives providing care at home and address other parts of the support system around people living with dementia.HFCUniverse takes brain health education to younger audiencesEducation became another major part of the charity’s activities in 2025, particularly through HFCUniverse, its online learning platform. The programme combines scientific information with entertainment to introduce high school and college students to brain health, Alzheimer’s disease and prevention.The platform is free to access and allows learners to complete courses at their own pace. HFC reported that more than 14,000 people had used HFCUniverse by the end of 2025, representing a 3,000 per cent increase since 2023.The charity also worked to turn some of those learners into advocates within their own communities. Its Youth Movement Against Alzheimer’s (YMAA) network had 100 chapters across the United States and internationally by the end of the year, following a 56.25 per cent increase in the number of chapters formed during 2025.A total of 77 young people were certified as Peer Brain Health Leaders through the programme’s curriculum. More than 2,000 students also engaged with the growing chapter network, learning about brain health and taking part in advocacy activities.The initiative gives young participants an opportunity to discuss dementia and prevention with their peers, rather than leaving those conversations solely to medical professionals and older generations.Documentary and community events extend the charity’s reachHFC also used film, live performances and conversations to introduce its work to wider audiences. One of its projects was Taking Care, a documentary examining the experiences of people caring for loved ones. The organisation hosted its Los Angeles premiere, bringing together caregivers, advocates and supporters for a screening and discussion.The film subsequently reached an estimated audience of more than 75,000 people by the end of the first quarter, through community screenings, educational partnerships, streaming services and national distribution. It became available on Amazon, Google Play and Apple TV, while a partnership with AARP helped extend its reach.Another initiative launched in 2025 was At the Table, a video series featuring caregivers, scientists, advocates and people personally affected by Alzheimer’s. The conversations addressed the realities of dementia, the responsibilities involved in caregiving and questions surrounding brain health.Live events remained an important fundraising route. HFC’s annual Friendsgiving gathering featured performances by Tig Notaro, Kumail Nanjiani, Hayley Williams and magician Asi Wind. The event raised $1.3 million for the organisation’s work supporting caregivers, expanding brain health education and helping families affected by dementia.Its community events also reached audiences in different parts of the country. In New York, the annual Comedy Night raised nearly $100,000. In Los Angeles, HFC Pride Night returned with Drag Bingo hosted by Laganja Estranja, with appearances by Seth and Lauren Rogen. The event generated more than $30,000 for caregiver programmes and inclusive resources for LGBTQIA+ families.A year of expanded support and public engagementThe organisation reported raising $31 million in 2025 to support family caregivers, brain health education and prevention research. Across its programmes, public events and online community, HFC reached approximately 4.4 million people.For Seth and Lauren Rogen, the organisation grew out of an experience within their own family. More than a decade after its establishment, Hilarity for Charity is working across several areas of Alzheimer’s support, with its 2025 report documenting the scale of that activity and the families and communities it aims to reach.You use AI every day. articles.title: Watch: 400 km above Earth, Nasa astronaut Anil Menon shows how he voted from space
articles.summary: Three Nasa astronauts, including Anil Menon, cast their ballots in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, from aboard the International Space
articles.body: Three Nasa astronauts, including Anil Menon, cast their ballots in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, from aboard the International Space Station (ISS), orbiting more than 400 km above Earth.Menon shared a video on X showing how astronauts can exercise their right to vote while living in space. He said he and fellow Nasa astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins completed electronic ballots and securely transmitted them to election officials."Yes, you can even vote from space!" Menon wrote in his post. "All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials."Nasa Administrator Jared Isaacman also praised the astronauts for participating in the November 3 elections despite being hundreds of kilometres above Earth.In the 29-second video, Menon, wearing an 'I voted' sticker, showed his sleeping compartment, which doubled as his polling booth."Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today," he said.Menon submitted his ballot to Harris County, Texas, which is home to Nasa's Johnson Space Center and Mission Control. According to the Associated Press, Delaney and Watkins also voted using the same process.Menon reached the ISS on July 14 aboard a Russian Soyuz mission, while Delaney and Watkins arrived on October 1 aboard a SpaceX rocket.The voting process uses Nasa's Near Space Network, managed by the Goddard Space Flight Centre in Greenbelt, Maryland. Ballots are encrypted and transmitted securely, with access restricted to the astronaut and the relevant election clerk to protect the integrity of the vote.US astronauts have been voting from space since 1997, when Texas passed legislation permitting citizens in orbit to participate in elections. Nasa astronaut David Wolf became the first to use the provision, casting his ballot from Russia's Mir space station.The US midterm elections are being held to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, 37 members of the Senate, 36 state governors and several local representatives.Meanwhile, the US Justice Department deployed around 1,000 election monitors and observers across all 50 states, describing it as the largest monitoring effort in its history. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon defended the deployment, saying the department was pursuing election transparency in an "assertive and nondiscriminatory manner".You use AI every day. articles.title: First polls close in pivotal US midterm elections
articles.summary: With control of the US Congress on the line, results from Tuesday’s races will have marked implications for the country.
articles.body:
After a full day of voting, the first polls have begun closing in the consequential US midterm elections .

Control of the US Congress is on the line, with all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats up for grabs .

Democrats, who have campaigned on promises to combat the country’s rising cost of living and end the US-Israel war on Iran, are eyeing a return to power in the US House. The party is also optimistic it could recapture control of the US Senate from Republicans when all ballots are counted.

The first clues to how the midterms may affect each party will appear in the US state of Kentucky’s highly competitive sixth congressional district, where polls closed at 6pm ET (23:00 GMT).

In the conservative district, which includes the state’s second-largest city, Lexington, Democrats have invested heavily in the campaign of US Navy veteran Zach Dembo, who is running against a Trump-backed physician and former state lawmaker, Ralph Alvarado.

If Republicans hold the seat, it could signal how the party may perform in other races across the country.

Results from all of the day’s races will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening. But some may not be known until Wednesday, or later, as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.

Follow all the returns on Al Jazeera’s live results page .

articles.title: Christa Pike asks court not to send her to former prison block following failed execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike claims her life is in danger if moved back to her former housing unit, citing severe weakness after surviving the botched lethal injection.
articles.body: Christa Pike, the death row inmate who survived a botched lethal injection attempt, has filed an emergency federal court motion to stop prison officials from transferring her back to her former housing block, claiming her life is in danger. Pike, 50, is currently in solitary confinement in the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville as she recovers from the execution attempt. In her court filing, Pike argued that her severe physical weakness leaves her vulnerable and unable to protect herself if returned to her previous unit, the New York Post reported. CHRISTA PIKE'S EXECUTION DOCTOR SAYS MISPLACED IV SENT LETHAL DRUGS INTO HER ARMS INSTEAD OF VEINS "This pod houses inmates with significant histories of assaults and disciplinary problems," the motion states. "In my two years living in this pod… I witnessed multiple assaults by close custody inmates of other inmates and guards, multiple individuals who were undergoing acute psychological breakdowns, and significant danger." Pike emphasized her inability to handle potential threats. "In my current physical condition, I could not defend myself or get away if another inmate attacked me," she wrote. "I am afraid that I will be seriously hurt if I am moved to that pod while I am this weak." CHRISTA PIKE DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, RETURNED TO PRISON AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION, ATTORNEYS SAY The motion further states that returning to her prior housing unit poses a "high risk of infection and further injury" due to unsanitary conditions, specifically noting that she would be forced to clean and use an alleged "roach-infested shower" on her own while still recovering, according to the Post. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow participant in a Job Corps training program in Knoxville. In 2001, she received an additional conviction for the attempted murder of another inmate. DEATH ROW KILLER CHRISTA PIKE DESCRIBES WAKING UP AFTER EXECUTION SHE NEVER EXPECTED TO SURVIVE Poised to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries, Pike survived after two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her during the Sept. 30 execution attempt. articles.title: Joe Rogan warns 'woke' ideology is replacing God on the left and entering into Christianity
articles.summary: Podcaster Joe Rogan argued woke ideology has become a replacement for religion, with LGBT pastors inserting non-biblical ideas into Christianity.
articles.body: Podcaster Joe Rogan argued Saturday that progressive ideology has replaced religion for many on the left and that some are injecting their political beliefs into Christianity. Rogan said he believed the left was "much more loony" than the right because a large portion of the left has embraced secularism. "Like when you think about the left, you generally don't think about like Christianity or any religion really. It's more of like a science-based like, ‘We're too smart for that thing.’ And I think they're just lost," Rogan said on his podcast. "There's no moral scaffolding to hold on to." TALARICO DISMISSES PAST COMMENTS ABOUT GOD AND GENDER AS 'PROVOCATIVE' WHILE INVOKING CHARLIE KIRK Rogan went on to argue that having a shared code like the Ten Commandments and showing humility toward a higher power are good for society. He said that for many liberals, far-left political ideology has become their new religion, to the point where they try to inject their liberal beliefs into traditional Christianity. "Another thing that's interesting with the religious thing when it comes to the left is there's been this larger than normal presence of these, like, LGBT pastors and these people that are promoting a very different Christianity," Rogan said. "They're talking about things that, you know, biblical scholars are like, ‘Hey, wait, what page is this on? What? Where does it say abortion's OK? Like, how are you getting to that? Where does it say God's non-binary?’" "You know, there's a lot of this weirdness — that this woke weirdness that sort of entered into religion and some pastors are doing it. And you go, ‘OK, is that good?’ I don't know if that's good," he said. "Because you're not following the original stuff." Rogan went on to say that if anything in the Bible is due for a modern reckoning, it would be biblical passages about slavery and genocidal warfare first, long before people try questioning God’s gender identity. EXPERT TEARS APART TALARICO'S VIRAL CLAIM HIS AGENDA IS BASED ON JESUS'S TEACHINGS: 'BUTCHERING THE BIBLE' His guest, "Triggernometry" co-host Francis Foster, agreed, recalling his Catholic upbringing and comparing it with a more modernized Church of England service. Foster said that if one is going to be religious, you want "the real deal," a faith that takes itself seriously. "You want to hear the Latin!" Rogan said. "You want the good stuff," Foster continued, noting that a genuine religion needs a sense of moral consequences for bad deeds and saying, "You want to sit there and think to yourself, ‘F---, I'm going to hell, and it's going to be awful.’" CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bishop Robert Barron, founder of Word on Fire and Bishop of Winona-Rochester in Minnesota, told Fox News Digital he largely agreed with the substance of Rogan's take. "For the past several decades, various forms of liberal Christianity have compromised the doctrinal content of the faith, first turning the great dogmas into vague symbols and subsequently evacuating them completely in favor of the progressive political agenda," he said. "The test is whether someone can honestly and with enthusiasm subscribe to the Apostles’ Creed. Does he believe in God, in the divinity of Jesus, in the power of the Holy Spirit, in the objective truth of the Resurrection? If not, he is using classical Christianity as a smokescreen."
